lesson.title: Removing and Reclaiming: The pop() Method
lesson.summary: The pop() method removes a key from a dictionary and returns its value in one step, optionally accepting a default so a missing key does not crash the program.
lesson.body:
Deleting an item from a dictionary is one thing; deleting it while also grabbing the value it held on the way out is another, and that second job is what pop() is built for. Calling dictionary.pop(key) does two things in one step: it removes key from the dictionary, and it returns the value that key was mapped to, so you can keep using it.

cart = {"pen": 2, "notebook": 1, "eraser": 3}
removed = cart.pop("notebook")
print(removed)
print(cart)

This prints 1, then {'pen': 2, 'eraser': 3}. The value that was stored under "notebook" is captured in removed before the key disappears, and the second print confirms that "notebook" is genuinely gone from cart, not just set to some empty value.

Just like get(), pop() supports an optional second argument that acts as a default, and that default changes what happens when the key does not exist.

missing = cart.pop("stapler", "not in cart")
print(missing)

This prints not in cart. Because "stapler" was never a key in cart, pop() cannot remove or return a real value for it, so instead it hands back the fallback string we supplied, and the dictionary itself is left unchanged since there was nothing to remove.

cart.pop("stapler")

This line, with no default supplied, raises a KeyError, because "stapler" is still not a key in cart and pop() has no fallback value to return instead. This mirrors exactly what you learned about get(): supply a default when a missing key is a normal, expected possibility, and skip the default only when a missing key should be treated as a real bug worth stopping the program over.
